interminable

/in-TUR-mih-nuh-buhl/ - the stress falls on TUR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Interminable means seeming to have no end.

The toddler judged the checkout line interminable and said so, at volume, in the only word he had: 'Done.'

Worked Example

The eighth-grade awards night was scheduled for one hour. There were certificates for attendance, for improved attendance, for very nearly perfect attendance; a slideshow; then a second slideshow correcting the first. Somewhere past the ninety-minute mark, time stopped behaving — parents swore the clock's hands were painted on. The evening was, in the only word for it, interminable.

Interminable measures the feel of time, not the fact of it: the evening did end, as evenings do. That is the word's little joke — in- + terminus, 'no end,' filed as a complaint against things that merely end too slowly. When something literally cannot end, everlasting makes the factual claim; interminable just rolls its eyes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

endless: Endless is the plain twin, and read literally it makes a bigger claim than interminable: truly without end. In everyday complaint the two swap freely, but interminable keeps a wink of honesty built in — the thing does end; it only behaves as if it never will.

never-ending: Never-ending is the everyday overstatement, first cousin to a groan — the never-ending meeting, the never-ending roadwork. Interminable files the same complaint in longer trousers: formal, faintly comic, and honest underneath, since the interminable thing does eventually terminate.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

brief: over quickly

short-lived: gone almost as soon as it starts

Where it sits · how close to never ending it comes — drawn-out → interminable → everlasting

drawn-out vs. interminable: A drawn-out speech runs long and everyone feels it; interminable turns the complaint all the way up — it seems to have no end at all.

everlasting vs. interminable: Everlasting outruns interminable: the interminable assembly does eventually end — it only feels endless — while the everlasting flame truly never goes out.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: not

Root — termin

Root — termin: end, boundary (Latin terminus)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: able to be

Put it together

Put it together: In- (not) + termin (end, from Latin terminus) + -able (able to be) = not able to be ended. Terminus was the Roman god of boundary stones, and his name still marks endings everywhere — terminals, term papers, the end of a term. Interminable borrows the god for comic effect: nothing mortal lacks an end, but plenty of meetings feel excused.

Use the root in a new word: terminal

Use the root in a new word: terminal: The last stop is called the terminal because the line ends there — terminus poured in concrete.

Word Choice

wry / complaining

Interminable files a complaint about felt time: the meeting, speech, or layover that outlives the sitting. It ends — it just doesn't seem to. For things that literally never end, everlasting makes the factual claim; interminable is the eye-roll, so don't spend it on anything you enjoyed.
